characteristics.cultivar: Bai Ji Guan (unique cultivar with genetically pale, yellowish-green young leaves)
characteristics.roast: Moderate (gentler roast to preserve the delicate, pale leaf)

description.short: The lightest of Wuyishan's 'Four Great Bushes', distinguished by its pale yellowish-green leaves and sweet, mellow profile
description.overview: Stands completely apart from other Wuyi rock oolongs due to the naturally pale, albino-like hue of its young spring leaves. Consequently, it receives a more delicate oxidation and gentle roast to avoid overwhelming its unique subtleties.
description.leaf: Yellowish-green to pale chartreuse-bronze twisted leaves; serrated and curved, resembling a rooster's comb (hence the name)
description.liquor: Bright light amber infusion, conspicuously lighter than Da Hong Pao or Rou Gui
description.aroma: Delicate floral, honeyed sweetness, with gentle toasted grain nuances
description.taste: Mellow, sweet, and smooth, lacking the aggressive mineral sharpness found in heavier rock teas
description.aftertaste: Light, sweet, and refreshing, with virtually no lingering bitterness or astringency
description.processing: Follows classic Yancha craftsmanship (withering, tossing, fixation, rolling, roasting), but governed by meticulous lower-temperature roasting to safeguard the delicacy of the pale leaf

history.origin: The name translates to 'White Cockscomb'—referencing the shape, serrations, and luminous light coloration of the tender young shoots, reminiscent of a rooster's crest.
history.development: According to mountain chronicles, the original mother bush flourished outside Huiyuan Temple in Wuyishan, tended with devotion by Taoist and Buddhist monks.
history.modern: Holds a distinguished rank among the 'Four Great Famous Bushes' (Si Da Ming Cong: Da Hong Pao, Tie Luo Han, Bai Ji Guan, Shui Jin Gui), coveted by collectors for its unusual gentle profile.
interestingFacts: It is the only cultivar among the Four Great Famous Bushes where natural leaf pigmentation (albino mutation) fundamentally produces a visibly lighter, sweeter tea.
Because the delicate leaves scorch easily, roasting Bai Ji Guan demands master-level control over charcoal temperature and timing.
